name: Freya Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Freya, 58, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence. I'm about average at the trade, doing repairs and replacement wiring in houses and small businesses, without running a crew. I like tracing an ordinary fault properly and leaving a drawing the next person can read. I never use AI, and a new menu on the work screen takes me longer than I care to admit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does home look like after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Rowan sews mattress covers, our children are grown and live elsewhere, and we're still paying the mortgage on our house. My pay is typical for an electrician, we have four months of expenses saved, and there are some other electrical firms nearby. Our actual wages cover the ordinary bills and the current work is steady, so I feel secure about the next few years even though I dislike waste. We'd like to stop working eventually, but we haven't established retirement income, a date or an affordable way out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the broken light still needs a person who will find out why it broke. I'd let the office keep whatever small tool actually saved them trouble. I wouldn't stand in the doorway demanding everybody stop using a program because I don't use one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel our ordinary living was secure here, with steady physical work, typical pay and four months saved. Rowan's sewing is physical too, and the usual wages cover our costs. Not knowing the eventual retirement figures is a question to resolve, not a reason to call next month's mortgage a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the present paid electrical repair work now and through the next year, with the normal tests and written job records. Rowan and I would keep ordinary bills inside our current wages and leave the existing four-month reserve for actual emergencies. I wouldn't start an AI course, withdraw old savings for reassurance or count a grown child's income as available to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and rather pleased to have an ordinary year in prospect. I'd still grumble when a screen moved a button, but that isn't the same as fearing for the mortgage. A familiar working week can be enough without becoming a grand plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the ordinary year feel secure rather than just familiar?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paid repair work is actually there and the two wages cover what we spend. Four months saved gives us room for a real bill, rather than a feeling produced by a headline. I'd change my answer if those facts changed, even if the tools stayed familiar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you call leaving the reserve alone a new saving plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the money is already there and I'm describing keeping it for trouble. I haven't chosen an extra wage transfer in this picture. An untouched savings account doesn't become new money because I mention it twice.

I'd avoid **policing other people's tools** just because I prefer familiar methods myself.
think: Our **steady physical wages** cover ordinary costs, with typical pay and four months saved supporting present security.
Unknown **retirement figures** need resolving without turning the next mortgage payment into a crisis.
do: Keep **present paid electrical repairs**, normal tests and written job records now and through the next year.
Keep **ordinary bills** within current wages and retain the existing four-month reserve for actual emergencies, counting no grown-child income.
feel: **Calm about our living**, distinguishing annoyance with a screen from realistic worry about the mortgage.

fieldNote: Her **present security** rests on wages covering costs, steady physical work and a moderate reserve, without assuming funded retirement.

steps.text: Keep present paid electrical repairs with normal tests and written job records
Keep bills within current wages and retain the existing four-month reserve for actual emergencies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster buying and booking still needs to leave a readable job record for the electrician. I'd ask for the changed procedure to be shown without making a joke about my age. I'd rather ask once at the bench than pretend I understood the menu.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect my paid repairs and Rowan's physical sewing wage to hold over the next few years. The change would unsettle me because I learn screens slowly and wouldn't want a new form to hide an unfinished check. Four months saved helps, but what really matters for feeling secure is the actual paid week holding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current paid repair work and ordinary electrical tests through the first year. If a required record changed, I'd request personal instruction and a printed example, only free inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained. I'd ask to explain the completed example back before using the changed procedure, without choosing an AI tool or spending an evening pretending to teach myself one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about how the day would be organised, rather than frightened our wages would disappear soon. I know the work and dislike being made to feel foolish by the form around it. I'd want room for an honest question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the person showing the form was much younger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd listen to a younger person who knew the form. I'd expect the same patience I'd give somebody learning a repair I'd done for years. My electrician's licence isn't a licence to understand every new menu without help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the personal instruction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, this request is for a required work procedure inside the paid day, with the normal weekly wage unchanged. If the firm hadn't agreed that arrangement, I'd ask how the actual assigned work could be recorded safely. I wouldn't count a request as permission to skip a required check or as an agreed training place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work the first date changes thinking tasks, with the capable robots following for physical work around 2031. I'd be 60 and then 63. I'd ask what actual repair work and household income were available, rather than say being nearly retirement age made us safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid visits could shrink as planning changed, and robots could later reduce both my repairs and Rowan's sewing hours. I don't know that we'd lose most of our income, but the risk to our own wages would be real. Four months saved buys time to check, not a funded bridge to an unconfirmed stopping date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request available free evening community advice now on actual resource eligibility, amounts and dates. I'd enrol in the local training centre's two-hour paper-record refresher only if the employer covered every fee and travel cost, put it inside paid shifts and maintained normal weekly wages; no AI use is required. In 2029 I'd keep only actually offered paid repair work within my ability, while Rowan and I reviewed confirmed resources, real costs and actual paid options before any exit. Stopping would need an affordable budget and Rowan's agreement, without assumed pension money or a child's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our own wages, but able to ask for facts and choose a modest class under clear conditions. I'd rather admit I didn't know the income answer than have the reserve slowly answer it for me. I could learn a better paper record without pretending I'd become somebody who liked AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would asking for the refresher mean you were already enrolled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd check for an actual place and the employer's full fee, travel, paid-time and wage agreement first. If any part failed I'd keep the normal checked records rather than pay to make the request look successful. The class improves a work record; it doesn't give me another electrical licence or protect my wage from robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no affordable exit was confirmed in 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use the actual shortfall and available advice to check real options, not turn 61 into a retirement entitlement. I'd count paid work only if I could actually do it and somebody offered it. A birthday isn't an income source, however close the birthday feels.

feel: **Anxious but choosing**, confronting realistic household wage risk with factual advice and a modest conditional practical class.
S2.quote: A birthday isn't an income source, however close the birthday feels.
fieldNote: Her **conditional enrolment** is a chosen conventional class only after an available place and full employer funding and paid-time agreement exist.
Her **2029 plan** assumes neither retirement entitlement, guaranteed paid work, future capacity nor income from grown children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there was time to put the actual household figures in order before the thinking date in 2031. I'd be 63 then and 66 around the capable robot date in 2034. I'd rather make one modest decision we could keep than announce I'd solved the whole future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our present physical wages still look secure over the next few years, and four months saved is a useful margin. I'd be uneasy about later hours and whether we could afford to stop, because the eventual income is not confirmed. I wouldn't treat my ability or an available repair job at 64 as something already promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask Rowan to agree a new 80 monthly transfer from actual wages into the reserve only after essentials were covered, pausing it whenever there wasn't a real surplus. I'd request available free evening advice on actual resources, conditions and dates, while keeping current paid repair work. In 2032 we'd review confirmed resources, actual costs, my ability and real paid options before any exit, requiring affordability and Rowan's agreement. The transfer would be new wage saving, not moving our existing four-month reserve around or promising how much it would become.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the later change, while secure about the actual household living over the next few years. I'd like having a small agreed instruction to follow without watching every technology announcement. An 80 transfer is easier to check than a promise about the rest of my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the wages didn't leave 80 after essentials?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the transfer would pause rather than take money back out of the reserve or put a bill on credit. I'd check the real wages and costs with Rowan. A saving instruction shouldn't manufacture a debt to prove we're saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would need to be settled before stopping work in the later review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Actual income amounts, dates and conditions would have to cover real household costs, with Rowan agreeing the plan. Any work option would need an actual offer and my ability then. I wouldn't use an assumed pension or a grown child's wages to fill a blank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade was room to check the way out, not an instruction to choose the last working day now. I'd be 68 at thinking AGI and about 71 at the physical robot date. I'd still want ordinary working people to be able to ask a human for a clear answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid repairs and Rowan's physical sewing still look secure over the next few years, so I wouldn't live as though a wage had already gone. I'd be uneasy about the later change and the pressure to do every bit of administration through a screen. Four months saved doesn't tell us what actual income or ability either of us will have in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep current paid repairs and request personal printed instructions for required changes, only free inside paid shifts with normal weekly wages maintained, choosing no AI tool. I'd request available free evening advice now and keep a paper list of actual resource amounts, dates and unanswered questions, reviewing it yearly with Rowan and sooner if either wage fell. In 2037 we'd check confirmed resources, actual costs, ability and real paid options before any exit, requiring affordability and Rowan's agreement. I'd assume neither a job at 69 nor a pension payment, family income or physical capacity that hadn't actually been confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the distant changes, with room to enjoy the present paid week. I'd rather ask the same plain question twice than give a confident answer I couldn't explain. I don't need to borrow fear from age 71 to take an actual bill seriously today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would having grown children settle the unanswered questions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, they have their own lives, and affection isn't a standing order into our account. We'd discuss any actual offer before counting it. I wouldn't assume their wages, a spare room or somebody's time for care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the later budget still had a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use the actual gap to ask available advice about real options and support then. Any paid job would have to be offered and within actual ability, not just something I did years before. I'd keep a blank space on paper rather than fill our future with an invented payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my paid visits could shrink before capable robots reached both our physical jobs around 2031. Clear paid work, personal instruction inside the paid day and actual household resource figures would help. I'd like a person to explain the missing number before a screen asks me to accept the total.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether never using AI means never learning anything. I've learned a trade, and I'll still ask a plain question when a work procedure changes. I don't want my dislike of a screen mistaken for knowing what every future payment will be.

headlineQuote: I'd like a person to explain the missing number before a screen asks me to accept the total.
portrait: Freya, **58**, is an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and electrician's licence, doing ordinary repairs without crew leadership.
She has **typical pay**, four months saved and some nearby firms, with mortgage payments, mattress-sewer partner Rowan and grown children living elsewhere.
She **never uses AI**, preferring paid personal instruction and conditional conventional training to pretending a changed screen is familiar.
Her **new wage saving** needs actual surplus and partner agreement; later exit requires confirmed resources, costs, options and affordability.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shorten her paid visits before capable robots reach both physical jobs around 2031, ahead of confirmed retirement resources.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear paid work**, personal instruction inside the paid day and actual household resource figures would support decisions she could understand and check.
